title: Portrait Photography Tips: Lens, Light, Focus and Settings — cv.cm
description: Portrait photography tips for the person holding the camera or phone: lens and aperture, eye focus, window light and open shade, backgrounds, angles and directing.
h1: How do you take good portrait photos?
answer: Stand back and use a short telephoto view (about 50 to 135 mm on full frame, or 2x to 3x on a phone), focus on the nearest eye, and put the person in soft light such as a window or open shade. Choose a plain background that is far behind them, shoot at eye level, and talk to your subject so the expression looks relaxed.

body: A good portrait has four things: a sharp eye, flattering light on the face, a background that does not compete, and a real expression. Gear helps with the first three, but the expression comes from how you work with the person. Most weak portraits fail on one of these four, so check them in this order before you press the shutter.
This page is for the person holding the camera. If you are the one in front of the lens, see the posing guide, and if you have no photographer at all, see the self-portrait guide.

Distance shapes a face more than the lens does. When you stand very close, the nose is much nearer to the lens than the ears, so it looks larger and the face looks narrow. Standing back about 1.5 to 3 m and using a longer focal length to fill the frame gives natural proportions. That is why 85 mm on a full-frame camera (about 50 to 56 mm on APS-C) is the classic portrait lens. A 50 mm lens works well for half-body and full-body shots, and 135 mm compresses the background further for tight head shots.

On a phone, the 1x main camera is a wide angle. For a head-and-shoulders photo, switch to the 2x or 3x lens and step back, or use portrait mode, which often picks a longer lens for you. Avoid pinching to zoom past the real lenses, because that only crops the image.

Aperture controls how much of the scene is sharp. Canon's portrait guidance gives three useful starting points: f/2.8 for a strongly blurred background, f/5.6 when you are close or using a telephoto and f/2.8 is too much, and f/8 to f/11 when you want everything sharp, such as a person in front of a landmark.

body: A simple way to work is aperture priority (A or Av) with auto ISO and a minimum shutter speed of 1/250 s. People move, even when they think they are still, and 1/250 s keeps blinks and small sways sharp. For the full background-blur story, see the aperture and depth of field guide. To try these combinations without a model, cv.cm's portrait camera simulator lets you change lens, aperture, distance and shutter speed on a simulated sitter and see the blur and motion change.

Viewers look at the eyes first. If the eyes are soft, the photo looks wrong even when the ears or the hair are sharp. Turn on face or eye detection autofocus if your camera has it. Without it, use a single focus point, place it on the eye nearest to the camera, and half-press to lock focus.

At f/1.8 or f/2 the zone of sharp focus is only a few centimetres deep at portrait distance. If the face is turned, the far eye will be soft. That is normal, but the near eye must be sharp. If you keep missing, close down to f/2.8 or f/4.

On a phone, tap the face on the screen before you shoot. Most phones also detect faces automatically. To keep focus and brightness fixed while you take several frames, touch and hold the face until AE/AF Lock (or a similar lock) appears.
Light matters more than the camera. Soft light comes from a large source close to the person, so shadows have gentle edges and skin looks smooth. Two free sources are always available.

ul: Window light: place the person 1 to 2 m from a window that does not get direct sun, turned about 45 degrees toward it. One side of the face is brighter and the other falls into a soft shadow, which shows shape. If the shadow side is too dark, hold a white card, a sheet of paper or a white wall on that side.
Open shade: on a sunny day, stand the person just inside the shade of a building or a tree, facing the open sky. The light is bright and even, with no squinting and no hard shadows under the eyes.
Golden hour: when the sun is low, the light is warm and soft. Put the sun behind the person for a glowing rim around the hair, and expose for the face.
Overcast days: clouds act like a giant diffuser. Colors are soft and skin looks even, which is good for beginners.

body: Avoid midday sun on the face. It causes squinting, dark eye sockets and a bright shine on the forehead. If you must shoot then, turn the person so the sun is behind them, and raise exposure compensation by about +0.7 to +1 EV so the face is not dark. Indoors under ceiling lamps, faces can look orange or green; see the white balance guide for the fix.

ul: Move the person away from walls. The farther the background is behind them, the more it blurs. Five metres or more makes a big difference even at f/4.
Check the edges of the frame for poles or trees that seem to grow out of the head, bright signs, and strangers. Take one step to the side to remove them.
Shoot at eye level, or slightly above for a head shot. Shooting from below makes the chin and nose dominant unless that is the effect you want.
For full-body shots, lower the camera to about waist or chest height. Shooting down from your own eye height makes legs look short.
Do not crop at joints such as knees, elbows, wrists or ankles. Crop between them, for example mid-thigh or mid-upper-arm.
Leave a little space above the head and place the eyes near the upper third of the frame. Turn on grid lines to help.

body: Vertical framing suits a single person. Horizontal framing suits couples, groups and environmental portraits where the place tells part of the story.
Most people feel awkward in front of a camera. Your words fix more photos than any setting. Show them the pose with your own body instead of describing it, and give one instruction at a time.

ol: Explain the plan in one sentence before you start, so they know how long it will take.
Start with easy shots: walking toward you, leaning on a wall, sitting. Movement relaxes the face.
Ask them to turn the body slightly away from the camera and the face back toward you. This is more flattering than square to the lens.
Ask for chin slightly forward and down. It defines the jawline.
Give the hands a job: hold a cup, a jacket, the strap of a bag, or touch the hair.
Talk and ask questions. Real smiles come in the second after a laugh, so keep shooting through it.
Show a good frame on the screen after a few minutes. It builds trust.

body.note: Ask before you photograph strangers, and before you post photos of anyone. In many places people have a right to control how their image is used. Before sharing, check that the photo does not reveal a home location; cv.cm's exif tool can remove GPS data from a file.

faq.q: What is the best focal length for portraits?
faq.a: On a full-frame camera, 85 mm is the classic choice for head-and-shoulders photos, with 50 mm for wider shots and 135 mm for tight faces. On APS-C, about 50 to 56 mm gives a similar view to 85 mm. On a phone, use the 2x or 3x lens rather than the 1x wide camera.

faq.q: Can I take professional-looking portraits with a phone?
faq.a: Yes, if you get the light and distance right. Use soft window light or open shade, step back and use the 2x or 3x lens or portrait mode, tap to focus on the face, and lower the exposure slightly if the skin looks too bright.

faq.q: Why are my portraits blurry even though focus looked right?
faq.a: Usually the shutter speed was too slow and the person or your hands moved. Use at least 1/250 s for people. If the eyes are soft but the ears are sharp, the problem is focus, not movement: use eye detection or a single focus point on the near eye.

faq.q: Should I use flash for portraits?
faq.a: A phone or built-in flash pointed straight at the face gives flat skin, red eyes and a dark background, so avoid it when there is other light. An external flash bounced off a white ceiling or wall, or fired through a softbox, can look natural and is useful when daylight is weak.

faq.q: What aperture should I use for a group photo?
faq.a: Use f/4 to f/5.6 for a single row and f/8 when people stand in two or more rows, so every face is sharp. Focus on someone in the middle row, about one third of the way into the group.
